title: Engineering Projects
text:
This page highlights engineering projects involving mechanical design, electronics, fabrication, instrumentation, controls, and experimental testing.



Harvey Mudd College | Spring 2026 | Team of 4
Designed and deployed an autonomous underwater vehicle to investigate how visible light intensity and spectral composition change with depth in coastal waters near kelp ecosystems.



Completed autonomous underwater vehicle used for coastal deployment and underwater sensor measurements.


Final AUV integrating the structural frame, electronics housing, propulsion system, and environmental sensors.



Designed and assembled the PVC structural frame and motor system
Integrated electronic components into the underwater platform
Designed and soldered circuitry for pressure and temperature sensing
Integrated a TCS34725 RGB sensor, MPX5700 pressure sensor, and thermistor with a Teensy 4.1
Implemented and tested autonomous depth-control behavior
Collected and processed depth-resolved environmental measurements
Supported coastal deployment and experimental troubleshooting




The complete project report documents the vehicle design, sensor circuitry, calibration, autonomous control, coastal deployment, and experimental results.
Open Full Project Report





Teensy 4.1 • MATLAB • Sensors • Circuit Design • Soldering • Data Acquisition • Feedback Control • Experimental Testing





Harvey Mudd College | Fall 2025 | Team of 4
Worked with a faculty client to design a lightweight, portable lectern that could be rapidly assembled and disassembled for classroom use.



Final assembled configuration.


Collapsed configuration for portability.





Interviewed the client to identify functional and human-factors requirements
Translated stakeholder needs into engineering specifications
Developed and evaluated multiple design concepts
Created SolidWorks models and engineering drawings
Fabricated and tested iterative prototypes
Evaluated setup time, portability, durability, and usability




The final design:

Achieved an average setup time of approximately 1.6 seconds
Supported loads greater than 12 lb
Used a collapsible five-panel structure
Included removable support wings and grip surfaces
Was produced for approximately $24 in prototype materials




The final SolidWorks drawing package documents the complete assembly, individual panels, support wings, fabrication details, process routing, and bill of materials.

Fabricated a functional hammer from raw stock while developing precision machining and manufacturing skills.



Finished machined hammer.


Completed hammer fabricated from raw stock using manual machining processes.



Machined hammer components using a mill and lathe
Used a bandsaw and other shop equipment for stock preparation
Worked from engineering drawings and specified dimensions
Maintained required dimensional tolerances during fabrication
Evaluated hardface hardness requirements after machining

title: William Ortega
text:
I am an Engineering student at Harvey Mudd College interested in fluid dynamics, propulsion, aerospace systems, and experimental engineering.
I currently conduct research in Harvey Mudd’s Flow Imaging Research Lab, where I study bio-inspired flapping-fin propulsion using thrust measurements, high-speed imaging, Particle Image Velocimetry (PIV), and MATLAB-based data analysis.
My current research investigates how fin orientation, geometry, and aspect ratio influence propulsive performance and wake dynamics. I will present this work at the APS Division of Fluid Dynamics Annual Meeting in November 2026.
Outside of research, I am a co-founder and Co-President of Harvey Mudd’s chapter of the Society of Hispanic Professional Engineers (SHPE).
I am currently interested in opportunities involving propulsion, fluid mechanics, aerospace engineering, experimental testing, and mechanical systems.

title: Research
text:
I conduct experimental research in Harvey Mudd College’s Flow Imaging Research Lab, studying bio-inspired flapping-fin propulsion and how fin geometry and operating conditions affect thrust production and wake dynamics.
My current work focuses on horizontal fin configurations and aspect-ratio effects, with comparisons to previously studied vertical, surface-crossing configurations.



Experimental setup for horizontal flapping-fin propulsion testing, including the tank, actuation system, load cell and fin, green laser, and high-speed camera.





The project investigates how changes in fin geometry and operating conditions influence propulsive performance.
Parameters I have worked with include:

Actuation frequencies from 1–3 Hz
Multiple fin thicknesses from 1/32 in to 1/8 in
Multiple fin aspect ratios and geometries
Horizontal and vertical fin orientations
Fully submerged and surface-crossing configurations




My work includes:

Running water-tank propulsion experiments across different fin configurations
Setting up and positioning high-speed cameras
Aligning the laser sheet used for Particle Image Velocimetry (PIV)
Modifying experimental setups for horizontal-fin testing
Adapting MATLAB thrust-processing code for horizontal configurations
Processing thrust and force data
Comparing thrust coefficients across experimental configurations
Performing PIV analysis to study velocity fields, wake structures, and vorticity






For each configuration, experimental trials are conducted across different operating conditions. Force measurements are processed in MATLAB to evaluate thrust performance and compare configurations.



Particle Image Velocimetry is used to visualize and quantify the flow generated by the fin.
My role in the PIV workflow includes:

Positioning and configuring the high-speed camera
Aligning the laser sheet with the measurement plane
Collecting high-speed image sequences
Processing experimental images
Analyzing velocity fields and vorticity structures





I am currently investigating how fin aspect ratio affects propulsion performance.
These experiments vary fin geometry while maintaining controlled operating conditions, allowing us to compare thrust production and wake behavior across different aspect ratios.



This work will be presented at the APS Division of Fluid Dynamics Annual Meeting in November 2026, focusing on horizontal-fin configurations and aspect-ratio effects in bio-inspired propulsion.
